title: Neither Arising Nor Ceasing
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Question: In the sutras and treatises, what does 'neither arising nor ceasing' mean? Does it mean eternal existence?

inline.s: Question: In the sutras and treatises, what does 'neither arising nor ceasing' mean? Does it mean eternal existence?
Answer:
The term 'neither arising nor ceasing' has two completely different meanings:
First, in the sense spoken of by the non-Buddhist paths, 'neither arising nor ceasing' means: it has existed from the very beginning and exists eternally.

Second, in the sense spoken of in the Buddha-Dharma, 'neither arising nor ceasing' means: all things are illusory and have never existed ('originally there is not a single thing'); since they never arose, there is nothing to cease.
The Buddha said: 'Herein no dharma arises, nor does any dharma cease; without arising and without ceasing — such is the true mark of all dharmas.'
(The Great Jewel Heap Sutra, fascicle 77)
In the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, the Sixth Patriarch gave an incisive instruction concerning the Buddha-Dharma's meaning of 'neither arising nor ceasing':
[Jian
(Xue Jian, the envoy sent by Empress Wu Zetian)
said: The Master speaks of neither arising nor ceasing — how does this differ from the non-Buddhist paths? The Master
(the Sixth Patriarch)

said: What the non-Buddhist paths call neither arising nor ceasing uses cessation to put an end to arising and uses arising to reveal cessation — thus cessation is still not cessation, and arising is said not to arise. What I call neither arising nor ceasing is that fundamentally there is no arising, and therefore there is also no ceasing — this is why it differs from the non-Buddhist paths.]

Xue Jian said: The Master speaks of neither arising nor ceasing — what difference is there between this and the non-Buddhist paths? The Sixth Patriarch said: What the non-Buddhist paths call neither arising nor ceasing uses cessation to put an end to arising and uses arising to reveal cessation; in this way, cessation is as if not ceasing, and arising is said not to arise. But what I call neither arising nor ceasing is that things have never existed from the very beginning ('originally there is not a single thing'), and therefore there is also no ceasing — this is why it differs from the non-Buddhist paths.

The 'neither arising nor ceasing' spoken of in the Buddha-Dharma means: all dharmas have never existed (since they have never arisen, there is nothing to cease) — this is the true mark of all dharmas (the actual state of all dharmas).
The Buddha Treasury Sutra, Chapter Two on Buddha-Recitation, says:
“What is called the true mark of all dharmas? It means that all dharmas are ultimately empty and without anything whatsoever.”
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“All living beings, within non-arising, deludedly perceive arising and ceasing, and therefore it is called transmigration through birth and death.”
The Golden Light Sutra says:
“Non-arising is true; arising is false. Foolish people drift and drown in birth and death. The Tathāgata's essence is true and without falsehood, and is called nirvāṇa.”
The Humane King Sutra says:
“All dharmas are by nature truly empty, neither coming nor going, without arising and without ceasing, identical with the true limit and equal to the Dharma-nature.”
In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra, fascicle 296,

the Buddha said: “Subhūti, in this great treasury of the prajñāpāramitā, it is not taught that any dharma, however slight, arises or ceases, is defiled or pure, is grasped or abandoned. Why is this? Because there is not the slightest dharma that can arise or cease, be defiled or pure, be grasped or abandoned.”
The Heart Sutra says:
“This is the empty mark of all dharmas: neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.”

Therefore, the 'neither arising nor ceasing' spoken of in the Buddha-Dharma is the true mark of all dharmas: originally there is not a single thing, so how could there be any arising or ceasing to speak of?
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra, Chapter Eleven on the Study of Illusion, says:

“The Buddha asked Subhūti: What do you think? Does an illusion have defilement or purity? No, World-Honored One. Subhūti! What do you think? Does an illusion have arising or ceasing? No, World-Honored One.”
